name: Ahikam
title: Official under King Josiah and protector of the prophet Jeremiah
summary: Ahikam, son of the scribe Shaphan, was a prominent official in the late kingdom of Judah. He belonged to the influential Shaphan family, which supported King Josiah's religious reforms and had close ties to the prophet Jeremiah. When the Book of the Law was found in the temple, Ahikam was among those the king sent to consult the prophetess Huldah about its contents and implications. He is especially known for intervening to protect the prophet Jeremiah from those who sought his life after the bold sermon at the temple—an act that proved decisive in enabling Jeremiah to continue his prophetic ministry. Ahikam's son Gedaliah was appointed by Nebuchadnezzar as governor over Judah following Jerusalem's fall in 586 B.C., testifying to the family's enduring political standing through one of the most dramatic periods in Judah's history.

keyEvents.title: Sent to the prophetess Huldah
keyEvents.description: After the Book of the Law was found in the temple during King Josiah's reign, Ahikam was sent as part of an official delegation to consult the prophetess Huldah about the book's content and its meaning for the people's future.

keyEvents.title: Jeremiah's Temple Sermon and the Threat to His Life
keyEvents.description: Jeremiah prophesied that the temple would become like Shiloh if the people did not repent. This bold sermon led priests, prophets, and the people to seize Jeremiah and demand his death.

keyEvents.title: Protection of Jeremiah
keyEvents.description: When Jeremiah's life was threatened after the temple sermon, Ahikam son of Shaphan intervened and prevented Jeremiah from being handed over to the people to be killed. His intervention was crucial for Jeremiah to continue his prophetic work.

keyEvents.title: Gedaliah, the Son, Appointed Governor
keyEvents.description: After the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam as governor over those remaining in Judah. Jeremiah was entrusted to Gedaliah's care, indicating that the family still played a protective role toward the prophet.

keyEvents.title: The Murder of Gedaliah
keyEvents.description: Gedaliah son of Ahikam was murdered by Ishmael son of Nethaniah. The assassination marked the end of the last Jewish self-rule in Judah and led the remaining people to flee to Egypt against Jeremiah's advice.

versions.summary: Ahikam was the son of Shaphan, who served as a scribe under King Josiah. He is best known for protecting the prophet Jeremiah from those who sought his life after his temple sermon. His son Gedaliah was later appointed governor over Judah following Babylon's conquest.
versions.title: Protector of the Prophet Jeremiah
versions.reason: [minor] The title is good and descriptive, but could also mention his role as a court official under King Josiah to provide a broader picture.; [major] The roles are incomplete. Ahikam was not just a general 'leader', but a court official at the royal court. He was sent as part of an official delegation to the prophetess Huldah. Roles such as 'court official' or 'official' should be added.; [minor] The events 'Protection of Jeremiah after the temple sermon' and 'Jeremiah's temple sermon and the threat to his life' overlap thematically. The last two events (about Gedaliah) strictly speaking concern more about the son than Ahikam himself. However, it can still be justified to include them for context.; [minor] The first event concerns primarily the father Shaphan, not Ahikam himself. It is contextually relevant, but could clarify that Ahikam is mentioned in this connection.; [minor] Ahikam's siblings include Elasa and Gemariah, both of whom are mentioned in Jeremiah. Some scholars discuss whether all of Shaphan's sons mentioned in the Bible are truly siblings, but the traditionally accepted names appear correct.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. There are interesting historical and archaeological details about the Shaphan family, including bullae (seal impressions) that have been found archaeologically.

versions.summary: Akikam was the son of the scribe Shaphan and a prominent court official in the late kingdom of Judah. He was among those King Josiah sent to consult the prophetess Huldah after the book of the law was found in the temple. Akikam is best known for protecting the prophet Jeremiah from those who wanted to kill him after his bold sermon at the temple. The family of Shaphan belonged to an influential circle of officials who supported Josiah's reforms and the prophet Jeremiah. Akikam's son Gedaliah was later appointed by Nebuchadnezzar as governor over Judah after the fall of Jerusalem, which testifies to the family's enduring political significance.
versions.title: Court Official under King Josiah and Protector of the Prophet Jeremiah
versions.reason: [minor] 'Hoffmann' is an unusual spelling/designation. The correct Norwegian word is 'hoffmann' or more precisely 'embetsmann ved hoffet'. The term 'hoffmann' can work, but 'embetsmann' is more precise and common in Norwegian. Moreover, Akikam is already referred to as 'hoffmann' in the roles and summary, so the title is consistent. Keeping it as is, but suggesting a small improvement.; [major] The reference 2 Kings 25:22 (bookId 12, chapter 25, verse 22) concerns the appointment of Gedaliah, but the verse mentions 'Akikam son of Shaphan' only indirectly. More precisely, the verse is correct — 2 Kings 25:22 actually states that Nebuchadnezzar appointed Gedaliah son of Akikam son of Shaphan over the people. The reference is accurate.; [minor] The event 'Gedaliah's murder and flight to Egypt' primarily concerns Gedaliah and not directly Akikam. It is legitimate to include this as context for Akikam's legacy, but it should be clarified that this happened after Akikam's time. The description already makes clear that it refers to the son.; [minor] The role 'leader' is somewhat generic. Akikam was specifically part of the king's delegation and a protector of the prophet. 'Protector' or 'royal envoy' could have been more precise roles.; [minor] Some Bible scholars also consider Jaazaniah (Ezek 8:11, 'son of Shaphan') to be a brother of Akikam, although this is uncertain. The listed siblings Elasa (Jer 29:3) and Gemariah (Jer 36:10-12) are well attested. It may be considered to include Jaazaniah, but since it is uncertain, it is acceptable to omit him.

footnotes.text: The name Ahikam (Hebrew: אֲחִיקָם, ʾAḥîqām) likely means 'my brother has risen' or 'my brother has stood up,' composed of אָח (ʾaḥ, 'brother') and קוּם (qûm, 'to rise'). Such theophoric or kinship-related names were common in ancient Israel and expressed gratitude or hope.

The Shaphan family was one of the most influential official families in late Judah. Several members are mentioned in 2 Kings and Jeremiah as officials connected to the prophet Jeremiah and the reform movement under Josiah. At least four of Shaphan's sons or grandsons held prominent positions in Judah's administration.

Archaeologists have discovered several bullae (clay seal impressions) from this period that can be linked to individuals mentioned in biblical texts. A bulla with the inscription 'Gemariah son of Shaphan' was found in the burnt administrative building in the City of David in Jerusalem, providing extra-biblical confirmation of the Shaphan family's existence and status.

Ahikam's protection of Jeremiah (Jer 26:24) occurred in a context where another prophet, Uriah son of Shemaiah, was brought back from Egypt and executed for similar prophecies (Jer 26:20–23). This contrast highlights the real danger to Jeremiah's life and the crucial importance of Ahikam's political influence.

Gedaliah's murder (2 Kings 25:25; Jer 41:1–3) is traditionally commemorated in Jewish practice through the Fast of Gedaliah (Tsom Gedaliah), observed on the third day of Tishri, the day after Rosh Hashanah. This fast day testifies to the catastrophic significance the murder had for the last remnant of Jewish self-rule in Judah.

The delegation King Josiah sent to the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:12–14) included several high-ranking officials, including Ahikam. The fact that the king turned to a female prophet rather than male prophets such as Jeremiah or Zephaniah, both of whom were active during this period, has been the subject of much discussion among scholars and theologians.
